name: From Clay to Alphabet: The Story of Writing and Lost Scripts
description: How people first pressed marks into clay, how alphabets spread, and how scripts such as Linear B and Egyptian hieroglyphs were lost and found again.

checkpoints.name: Marks on clay and stone
checkpoints.note: Scribes in Sumer, Egypt, the Indus Valley and China invent writing independently. Some scripts, like cuneiform and hieroglyphs, serve for thousands of years, with Egyptians writing on papyrus; others, like the Indus signs, stay silent.

checkpoints.name: The alphabet spreads
checkpoints.note: Phoenician traders spread a short set of letters around the Mediterranean. The Greeks add vowels, the Etruscans and Romans pass it on, and in India Brahmi gives rise to many scripts.

checkpoints.name: Scripts of faith and empire
checkpoints.note: Runes and ogham mark the northern lands, Arabic script travels with the Quran, and Cyrillic is made for Slavic peoples. Egyptian hieroglyphs and many other old scripts die as their temples close.

checkpoints.name: Scripts made on purpose
checkpoints.note: In 1443 King Sejong's scholars create Hangul so that ordinary people can learn to read quickly. The Maya script falls silent under Spanish rule, and its decipherment must wait centuries.

checkpoints.name: Lost scripts found again
checkpoints.note: Using the Rosetta Stone, Champollion reads hieroglyphs in 1822, Ventris reads Linear B, and Sequoyah, Braille and Zamenhof show that new systems can be built by one person. Some scripts, like Linear A and the Indus script, still resist.
